2026 SEMA Show • 2027 Toyota Crown Signia Gets GT-S Concept Treatment for SEMA, Becomes a Sleek Wagon
Billionaire Rocket Pioneer Sir Peter Beck Becomes the Proud Owner of a Jetson One
8 photos
Photo: Jetson Aero
With its entire 2026 and 2027 production sold out a while ago, it’s crystal clear that everyone wants a Jetson One, but the fact that some of these owners are amazing tech innovators on their own proves that this contraption is far more than a trendy personal aircraft. The Jetson One is making history, and even Rocket Lab CEO Peter Beck agrees.
A year ago, the maker of the Jetson One personal eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) made headlines with the announcement of the first official owner of the Limited Edition Jetson One. That man was 33-year-old Palmer Luckey, founder of the defense tech startup Anduril Industries.
Luckey was one of the first to order a Jetson personal aircraft, and to trust in this groundbreaking technology. He was also willing to wait patiently for the delivery, as someone who understands the inevitable challenges that any tech startup faces in the beginning. He was supposed to get his Jetson One in 2023, but that ended up happening in September, 2025.
Jetson’s CTO Tomasz Patan and CEO Stephan D’haene flew to Carlsbad, California, to guide Luckey on his first Jetson One flight – although he turned out to be a natural who needed minimal training.
Now, an even more famous owner is making Jetson’s CTO and CEO proud. It’s none other than Sir Peter Beck himself, founder and CEO of Rocket Lab. What started as a small company is now the third most frequent orbital launcher in the world, after SpaceX and the Chinese government, after moving its headquarters to California more than a decade ago.
The Electron rocket, widely considered one of the most successful launch vehicles of all time, turned Sir Peter Beck into a rocket pioneer.
The New Zealand native who used to build rockets in his free time is currently a billionaire and a knight (he was appointed a Knight Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2024, becoming Sir Peter Beck). And, while Rocket Lab is working on what is claimed to be the world’s largest carbon composite rocket, Neutron, Sir Peter is getting ready for some personal fun aboard his Jetson One.
According to Jetson, Sir Peter’s Jetson One (a Founders Edition unit) was already delivered and he could take to the sky by Christmas, as soon as regulatory approvals kick into place.
For the Jetson team, this comes as a powerful confirmation and tribute. Before ordering his own, Sir Peter flew the Jetson One during a California visit and was immediately convinced. He applauded the Jetson engineers for making complex vertical electric flight “effortless and intuitive”, also speaking of the “sheer joy of flight” he experienced with the Jetson One.
The Jetson One is currently priced at $148,000 (without taxes) and available for order, with earlier deliveries set for 2028.

The New R36 Nissan GT-R Is Finally Here, Albeit Only in Spirit – Rendering
13 photos
Photo: Instagram | paolomariagaravaglia
It’s been more than a year since the R35 Nissan GT-R was put to sleep, but the model will return to the automotive world with an entirely new generation, and when it does, it should dwarf its predecessor in all aspects.
Rumor has it that the next generation should come out of hiding officially before the turn of the decade, perhaps the odd one, though some believe that it might actually be a couple of years away from being unveiled. This is contradictory data, and to be honest, it’s not exactly a surprise, because the Japanese company wants to keep most things about this model a secret until the big day comes.
Initial rumors spoke about an all-electric future for the upcoming Nissan GT-R . Needless to say that fans weren’t too happy about it, and since the automaker still listens to its customers, not to mention the fact that the EV market is experiencing a quite sharp divergence by region, has made the automaker reconsider this plan. Thus, ladies and gents, the R36 will not go down the zero-emission route.
A report dating back to six months ago revealed that the model will indeed avoid the EV route completely, as it will still feature an internal combustion lump. Chances are we are looking at a V6 of some sort, perhaps with twin turbocharging. And in order to keep the emissions in check and make the powertrain punchy, it might be assisted by electric trickery, either in the form of a self-charging hybrid or maybe a plug-in hybrid, though we’d lean on the former rather than the latter at this point.
Photo: Instagram | paolomariagaravaglia This recipe should be just about right for a modern-day sports car that will also target the new-age supercar segment in its top form(s), and fans should be happy that the next-generation Nissan GT-R won’t become an EV . Unless they actually dig zero-emission cars, of course. But what about the design part? Well, chances are it might borrow some styling cues from the Nissan Hyper Force Concept .
You do remember the study unveiled roughly three years ago, don’t you? It pretty much looked like a Nissan GT-R from the future, at least toward the rear, because the front fascia was kind of quirky. It featured a very sharp-looking bumper, had a canopy-like design, albeit without the canopy, obviously, cameras instead of side mirrors, an evolution of the R35’s taillights, a large rear wing, and a very aggressive diffuser. And it definitely sent Bosozoku vibes.
Quite strangely, the car manufacturer hasn’t gone into specifics when it comes to the powertrain, but it did announce that the Nissan Hyper Force Concept featured a solid-state battery that feeds electrons to an electric setup. The assembly can generate up to one megawatt of power in total, and this equals 1,340 brake horsepower (1,360 ps).
The study featured a lot of carbon fiber in its body, had a lightweight construction, produced tons of downforce, and had electric all-wheel drive. And while it did look like a Nissan GT-R from the future, from certain angles anyway, not everyone was a fan of the overall design. But worry not, fellow gearhead, because the final production model will definitely be toned down a lot.
Photo: Instagram | paolomariagaravaglia Could it look like the vehicle pictured in the gallery? Well, first things first, this thing came from @paolomariagaravaglia on Instagram, and it is deemed as an R36 Nissan GT-R Concept. And second and more importantly, the answer to this question is likely no. After all, no one who is not directly involve in its development knows anything about it, and this also includes the design.
The car in question kind of looks like a Nissan GT-R , though due to the overall proportions, it seems to be on the quite small side of things. Moreover, due to some of the styling cues, it reminds us of other models from different brands, and here, we’d say Audi and Peugeot. The front fascia does not really do justice to the iconic GT-R nameplate, and to be honest, neither does the profile.
The only things that somewhat reminds us of the R35 are the taillights, and perhaps the rear pillars, and the rear bumper seems to have been inspired by the R8, whereas the roof sends some TT vibes when looking at it from the front. As for the face, it could easily be mistaken for a Peugeot with a few styling tweaks. The wheels were somewhat inspired by the ones equipping the above-mentioned study, with an obvious emphasis on the word “somewhat.”
We (or I in this case) hope that this virtual concept does not end up influencing the actual car in any way, because the upcoming R36 Nissan GT-R has some very big shoes to fill, and this one just does not tick that box. Nevertheless, that does not make it an interesting CGI project, and that’s why we decided to share it with you. But do you actually like the design? source_document.body:
Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tries on new shoes he bought before tabling the 2026 budget. Credit: Finance Canada via X.
By: Colin McClelland and Frederic Tomesco November 5, 2026
Canada plans to extend two mineral exploration tax credits by five years and add antimony to the more generous incentive as Ottawa seeks to turn mineral deposits into domestic production and processing capacity.
Thursday’s federal budget proposes keeping the 15% Mineral Exploration Tax Credit and 30% Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit available through March 31, 2032, providing an estimated $956 million (US$684 million) in support over five years. Ottawa also proposes $424.4 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, to renew the Canadian Critical Minerals Strategy.
“But for too long, Canada has fallen behind in bringing those minerals from mine to market,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in Parliament. “That is why we are focused on increasing Canadian production and processing of our minerals.”
The package addresses both ends of mining’s investment problem: raising money for discoveries and securing the power, infrastructure and financing needed to develop them. The extensions would give junior explorers a longer financing horizon, while broader electricity and capital-investment measures could help projects move towards construction. Much of the larger funding architecture, however, was announced before budget day.
Surging deficit
Ottawa projects a $62.3-billion deficit in 2026-27, up from $39.3 billion last year, with annual shortfalls continuing through 2030-31. Federal debt is forecast to reach $1.37 trillion this fiscal year and $1.59 trillion by the end of that period, remaining around 40% of gross domestic product. Annual debt-servicing costs would rise to $85.5 billion from $60.2 billion over the same period, according to the Department of Finance.
Running another deficit with no credible plan to return to budgetary balance amounts to mortgaging future generations, said Gabriel Giguère, a senior policy analyst at the Montreal Economic Institute think tank.
“Each new dollar of debt generated by this budget is a dollar borrowed from Canada’s future generations,” Giguère said in e-mailed comments. “This reduces their room to manoeuvre in financing their own priorities, whether new spending or tax cuts.”
Ottawa is counting on stronger revenues and lower spending elsewhere to help finance the package, while continuing to borrow to cover annual deficits. Revenue projections have risen by an average of $23.9 billion a year over five years compared with the spring outlook, supported by higher oil prices, corporate profits, wages and consumption, according to the Department of Finance. Lower projected program expenses also create room, although some of that reflects delayed spending and lower take-up of existing programs rather than permanent cuts.
Exploration runway
Both exploration credits are currently due to expire next March 31. The proposed extensions would cover eligible flow-through share agreements entered into on or before March 31, 2032, according to the budget’s tax annex.
Flow-through shares let companies transfer eligible exploration and development expenses to investors, who can deduct them from taxable income. The exploration credits provide an additional benefit to individuals financing qualifying grassroots exploration in Canada.
Antimony’s inclusion in the 30% credit would apply to expenditures renounced under eligible agreements entered into after budget day and through March 31, 2032. The credit rate isn’t affected by the move.
The renewed critical minerals strategy would support mining and processing technology, geoscience and research, and targeted funding for priority projects. Ottawa also proposes $34 million over four years, starting in 2027-28, to renew GeoNorth, which provides public geoscience information for northern exploration, infrastructure planning and environmental assessments.
Helium producers would receive separate relief. Ottawa proposes treating eligible helium exploration, development and resource-property acquisition expenses like those in conventional oil and gas, effective for spending incurred on or after budget day. The government estimates the change would provide $54 million in tax relief over four years from 2027-28.
Power and processing
For miners and processors seeking reliable electricity, the budget proposes extending the Clean Technology and Clean Electricity investment tax credits to the end of 2040. The clean technology credit’s reduction to 15% would occur in 2040 instead of 2034.
“Canada has a head start: our grid is already 80% clean, and our electricity is among the most affordable in the G7,” Champagne said.
Eligibility for the clean electricity credit would also expand to the highest-voltage transmission lines within each province, for property acquired and available for use on or after budget day. That could help finance infrastructure serving new mines and industrial developments.
Ottawa proposes nearly $4 billion over 10 years, starting in 2027-28, for electricity infrastructure, renewable energy and priority power projects. A further $37 million in 2027-28 would support analysis of interprovincial connections and discussions about sharing their costs.
“We’re working with provinces, territories, and Indigenous partners to double Canada’s grid capacity by 2050,” Champagne said. “We will connect provincial grids. We will build thousands of kilometres of transmission lines. We will develop the nuclear energy sector.”
Canadian industrial suppliers could benefit from proposed domestic-content bonuses. The government plans 60 days of consultations on additions of up to 10 percentage points to the clean technology credit and five percentage points to the clean electricity credit. Their scope and conditions remain to be determined.
The budget also reaffirms the Productivity Mega Deduction announced in September. It would permanently allow immediate writeoffs for a broader range of capital assets and increase the deduction rate for Canadian development expenses to 100% from 30% on a declining-balance basis. The government puts the economy-wide fiscal cost at $36 billion over five years.
Mining investors wouldn’t qualify for every new incentive. The proposed Canada Growth Incentive would exempt up to $15 million in capital gains per qualifying individual per business, subject to eligibility conditions, but the tax annex explicitly excludes mining businesses. Utilities, financial services and several other sectors are also excluded.
Approval to construction
Ottawa is proposing $187.4 million over five years from 2026-27, plus $24.2 million in future years, to launch and operate a major projects management entity and begin supporting the Mackenzie Valley Highway and Taltson Hydro Expansion in British Columbia.
The entity would provide technical and project-development expertise to help approved projects advance.
“We are already moving major projects forward, with 28 nation-building initiatives referred to the Major Projects Office, including projects in energy, critical minerals and transportation,” Champagne said. “And with Budget 2026, we are building on that progress.”
The budget also reiterates the “one project, one decision, one year” approach in legislation introduced in September. The proposed federal deadline would start after proponents provide all required studies and information; it is not a one-year clock running from a project’s first announcement. Ottawa says Indigenous rights, consultation duties and treaty obligations would remain intact.
For project financing, the budget sets out the structure of the Canada Strong Fund, announced in the spring economic update. Ottawa plans to seed it with $25 billion over three years and introduce legislation establishing an arm’s-length Crown corporation.
The fund would invest alongside private capital on commercial terms. One illustrative model pairs a Canada Infrastructure Bank loan for road and power infrastructure with an opportunity for the fund to invest in a critical minerals developer. The example is a financing model, not an announced project investment.
Bank merger
Ottawa also proposes merging Export Development Canada and the Business Development Bank of Canada into a single federal development bank, combining support for domestic growth and international expansion. A specially constituted board would oversee the transition, with existing products and services maintained.
The government expects its financing Crown corporations to take greater risks than private lenders, potentially widening financing options for mining, processing and infrastructure projects.
For tariff-hit processors and manufacturers, Ottawa says support under the Regional Tariff Response Initiative has reached nearly $3.5 billion, including additional assistance for steel, copper and aluminum. The program offers support for productivity improvements, market diversification and liquidity.
The distinction between financing announcements and operating projects remains central. Ottawa identifies more than $44.6 billion in critical minerals projects under construction or with completed impact or environmental assessments, using 2025 data and selected 2026 projects. The budget’s new exploration and power measures aim to help enlarge that pipeline and move more of it into production.

1,300-HP C6 Corvette 427 Turbo Hits 200 Mph in Fourth Gear, Packs Classic 6-Speed Manual Tranny
71 photos
Photo: Youube/Autotopia LA
What's the most performant C6 Corvette ever? Kelly Bise and his 2,200+ hp record-breaker comes to mind, but here's another wild build, with a tamer 1,300-hp setup (on the lowest boost setting). While Bise piloted his twin-turbocharged 2009 Chevrolet Corvette Z06 to a standing-mile world record of 280.025 mph in May 2026, Arizona enthusiast Anoeil Atenousazar rules public highways in an equally audacious street machine.
Atenousazar's 2007 Chevrolet Corvette Z06 is an exercise in mechanical no-holds-barred excess. Known online as DaBossGarage, Atenousazar originally purchased the blue coupe equipped with an F-1X ProCharger supercharger and an ice box. Preferring exhaust-driven boost, he commissioned close friend Rudy Romero of Street Life Performance to ditch the blower and construct a hoodless, show-quality single-turbocharged highway roll-racing weapon instead.
This C6 is the apple that fell so far off the tree, it’s closer to oranges now. To appreciate the magnitude of this transformation, let’s recap the sixth-generation Corvette's factory pinnacle, the C6 ZR1. Built across five model years from 2009 to 2013, General Motors assembled 4,684 units of the flagship coupe, carrying a base MSRP of $103,300 in 2009 that rose to $112,575 by 2013.
Nicknamed the Blue Devil, it was the first production Corvette to eclipse both $100,000 and the 200-mph barrier in factory form.
Photo: YouTube/Autotopia LA Beneath its polycarbonate-windowed carbon-fiber hood, the stock C6 ZR1 housed a 6.2-liter LS9 V8 with a 2.3-liter Eaton supercharger, generating 638 hp (647 PS) at 6,500 rpm and 604 lb-ft of torque (819 Nm) at 3,800 rpm. Mated to a 6-speed Tremec TR6060 manual transmission, it hit 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, ran the quarter-mile in 11.3 seconds at 131 mph, and reached 205 mph, outpacing the original 505-hp 7.0-liter LS7 in Atenousazar's 2007 Z06.
But now, even that once-mighty ZR1 pales beside the forced-induction hardware protruding from Atenousazar's engine bay. Dominating the sightline is a Pro Mod-spec Garrett G57-3000 turbocharger, engineered for 3.0-liter to 12.0-liter engines and rated for 1,400 hp to 3,000 hp at 74,500 rpm (scroll speed, if it needs be said).
Featuring a 16-mm dual ceramic ball-bearing cartridge and a 106-mm compressor wheel, Atenousazar's unit pairs its 106-mm trim with a 122-mm inducer and a massive 140-mm hot side housing.
Photo: YouTube/Autotopia LA Surprisingly, the powerplant fed by this colossus is not an exotic billet race block. Instead, it is a 427-cube (7.0-liter) LS7 V8 built with off-the-shelf forged rods and pistons, topped by standard four-bolt Air Flow Research LS7 cylinder heads rather than six-bolt castings. Retaining the factory dry-sump lubrication system routed to rear catch cans, the motor limits output until a dedicated 3,000-hp version 2.0 engine is completed for the car.
Managing airflow from the Garrett snail requires heavy-duty plumbing finished in striking gold to contrast the blue bodywork. Pressurized air exits the compressor through 4-inch outer-diameter piping into a front-mounted 6-inch intercooler before passing two Tial blow-off valves and entering a Holley intake manifold.
Exhaust gases are regulated by twin 66-mm Precision wastegates and vented through a pie-cut titanium up-pipe that dumps raw fumes – and every so often fiery blazes of plasma - directly ahead of the windshield glass.
Photo: YouTube/Autotopia LA Supporting those airflow demands is a fuel system anchored by a 10.0-gallon-per-minute Aeromotive brushless pump supplying 2,600-cc injectors through leak-free PTFE lines with AN fittings. Granatelli coils and throttle-body hardware do double shifts alongside a Holley Dominator engine management system programmed with zero traction control.
At 15 psi of boost, the Z06 produces 1,300 hp, while two gold nitrous bottles sit disconnected in the trunk because boost alone proves sufficiently violent already.
Rather than converting to an automatic transmission like most four-figure-horsepower roll racers, Atenousazar insisted on shifting gears manually. Power flows through a Monster Clutch Co. triple-disc clutch and lightweight flywheel into an RPM Transmissions Level VII TR6060 6-speed manual gearbox and an RPM-built rear differential.
Photo: YouTube/Autotopia LA Custom tall highway gearing renders stoplight launches useless but stretches second gear to 120 mph, third past 180 mph, and fourth beyond 200 mph effortlessly. There’s a reason for that parachute strapped to the tail, but I know you want to know what happens in sixth just as much as I do. Shawn Davis, the host of Autotopia LA YouTube channel, can tell you more about how it feels to ride shotgun at abominable speeds, gazing at the closest thing to the hot hinges of you-know-what all the time.
Planting that fury to the pavement is a staggered Weld Racing wheel package featuring 15-inch rear beadlocks wrapped in 29-inch-tall 325/50R15 Mickey Thompson ET Street R drag radials and skinny front runners chosen deliberately to make high-speed handling feel livelier. Factory front Z06 brakes, a rear 15-inch small-brake conversion, and lowered suspension geometry work with a rear drag wing and parachute, which Atenousazar deploys after 215-mph to 220-mph blasts.
Externally, the Z06 retains stock body panels accented only by a carbon-fiber front lip, carbon-fiber side skirts, and updated headlights. Inside, the gearhead shunned racing buckets and roll cages to fit his voluminous frame comfortably in the factory leather seats.
Photo: YouTube/Autotopia LA Stripped of air conditioning and heating, the cockpit features a Holley digital dash, a console parachute lever, and an NRG steering wheel carrying rolling anti-lag and 30-psi scramble boost buttons instead.
Taking the monster onto Arizona thoroughfares from the Fat Fender Garage facility, Atenousazar and Davis initially cruised with coolant temperatures steady between 200 degrees and 205 degrees Fahrenheit despite 90-degree ambient heat.
When the engine stumbled under throttle after a recent spark-plug change, Romero summoned their local tuner. Within two hours’ time, a diagnostic revealed the throttle position sensor was reading 4 percent at idle, requiring a quick electronic reset.
Once recalibrated, the Z06 unleashed its full fury across three ferocious passes on its lowest 1,300-hp setting. Running out of pavement before fourth gear, Atenousazar's creation is one helluva machine that would definitely earn a place at the hightable at SEMA, if only for the furnace-sized turbo alone.

Buick Electra Leaks Online: This Is What You're Missing, America!
7 photos
Photo: Buick China
The first photos of the upcoming Buick Electra GS PHEV sedan hit the internet and you can’t but sit and wonder: why in the world isn't General Motors building this sedan in the United States for its home market?
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has leaked the official product images and filing data for the upcoming Buick Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan. Developed by the SAIC-GM joint venture, the large, fastback-style sedan is tailored specifically for the Chinese market and is very unlikely to ever set wheels on American land due to regulatory hurdles and prohibitive tariffs.
The production version represents a significant departure from the much taller, hatchback-like Electra GS Concept that made its debut in April 2025 as a preview of a future production model. And this is it! It may not be the concept car’s identical twin, but it is the next best thing.
With styling that pays tribute to Buick’s iconic Gran Sport lineup, the Electra GS PHEV car features ultra-slim, C-shaped LED headlights linked by an LED strip. The Buick tri-shield logo sits right below on a less aggressive "shark-nose" front fascia.
Photo: Buick China The Electra comes with a sleek, sporty, fastback roofline and streamlined silhouette, while the rear end gets taillights that stretch from one side to the other of the liftgate before curving inward, a layout that sends Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus vibes.
The Electra GS is the slightly shorter and potentially more affordable alternative to Buick’s existing Electra L7 Sportback sedan. It measures 190.0 inches (4,980 millimeters) in length, 75.4 inches (1,915 millimeters) in width, and 58.9 inches (1,495 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 112.8 inches (2,865 millimeters). Those numbers make it slightly smaller than the Buick Electra L7.
The leaked documents confirm the plug-in hybrid setup, which combines the electric motor, good for 221 horsepower (224 metric horsepower), with either the naturally aspirated 1.5-liter or the turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four. The naturally aspirated engine produces 72 horsepower (73 metric horsepower, while the turbocharged unit churns out 154 horsepower (156 metric horsepower).
The base variant rolls off the production line with 318 horsepower (322 metric horsepower), while the range-topping turbocharged example sees the light of day with a combined system output of 375 horsepower (380 metric horsepower).
Photo: Buick China The car is equipped with a Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery pack, produced in-house by SAIC-GM Powertrain Technology. However, GM has yet to disclose its capacity and how far the PHEV sedan can drive on electric power only.
GM hasn’t revealed any pricing details either, but it will most likely happen closer to the launch date set for early 2027.
While the Buick Electra GS PHEV will stay away from the U.S., it has every chance to make it to the European market.

He Bought This 1964 Mercury M-250 Pickup Truck for $900 After It Sat Parked for 40 Years
17 photos
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage
A car enthusiast, who has worked miracles on vehicles before, bought a 1964 Mercury M-250 pickup truck and is trying to return it to its former glory. The truck hasn't set wheels on the road for the past 40 years! In the meantime, its hood developed an entire ecosystem.
1987. That was when this 1964 Mercury M-250 pickup truck was last registered. It hasn't hit the road since. Brad Blakley of Grit & Iron Garage found it on Facebook Marketplace. He has never owned a Ford-built vehicle before, but there is always a first time for everything.
And it looks like he has started on the right foot, because Mercury trucks are quite an interesting chapter of Ford trucks’ history book. Ford produced a distinct lineup of Mercury-branded trucks from 1946 to 1968 specifically for the Canadian market. This allowed Canadian Lincoln-Mercury dealers to sell trucks alongside luxury cars.
By 1964, these trucks featured unique styling cues, like a distinct grille layout and Mercury lettering, while sharing the robust mechanics of Ford's legendary F-Series. The 1964 Mercury M-250 was sold exclusively in Canada. It was never offered by Ford Motor Company for sale to the general public in the United States.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage Back in mid-20th-century Canada, rural communities were massive, but populations were sparse. Ford Motor Company had two distinct dealership networks in Canada: Ford-Monarch and Lincoln-Mercury-Meteor.
Ford was worried about losing ground to General Motors, because many small towns only had one or the other. If a town only had a Lincoln-Mercury dealer, the residents of the area couldn’t buy a Ford F-Series truck. So Ford of Canada came up with the Mercury M-Series in 1946.
While the light-duty M-100 matched the light-duty Ford F-100, the M-250 was the heavy-duty 3/4-ton equivalent of the Ford F-250 . Ford sold hundreds of thousands of F-Series trucks in the U.S. and Canada, but Mercury M-Series trucks were sold strictly in Canada and only a fraction of those numbers. Finding a heavy-duty M-250 variant today is exceptionally rare.
Mechanically, the 1964 Mercury M-250 was built identically to the 1964 Ford F-250 as the firm made sure that parts were completely interchangeable. It was a robust, no-nonsense workhorse designed to handle brutal Canadian winters and rough farm terrain.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage The base engine was the 223-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) inline-six, the so-called "Mileage Maker," producing 135 horsepower (138 metric horsepower). The optional engine was the 352-cubic-inch (5.8-liter) FE Big-Block V8 with 220 horsepower (224 metric horsepower). A heavy-duty four-speed manual or a three-speed Cruise-O-Matic automatic put the power down.
The siblings rolled off the same production line, but came with distinct designs, starting with the grille. While the Ford trucks came with the massive "FORD" lettering across the front end, the 1964 Mercury grille featured the typical chrome format, and the front edge of the hood featured wide, individual chrome letters spelling out "MERCURY."
The Mercury truck was phased out in 1968, three years after the United States and Canada signed the Automotive Products Trade Agreement, which eliminated tariffs on vehicles built between the two countries, allowing Ford to cross-ship vehicles seamlessly across the border.
Because dealerships could now easily get whatever inventory they needed from either side of the border, the logistical need to manufacture a separate, low-volume Canadian truck line vanished. Production of the Mercury M-Series was officially halted in 1968.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage The truck that Brad ended up with is part of this story. The light-blue vehicle was originally listed for 1,000 Canadian dollars, but he negotiated it down to 900. He drove to the owner’s home with his new (well, not exactly new!) trailer to pick it up. He found it sitting behind some greenery, and by the way it looks, Mother Nature must have started to claim it.
Moss is growing on the hood, as if it’s indicating north with determination. Now, in Brad’s yard, it doesn't run, it doesn't drive, and it is sitting on flat tires, but the front bumper, which he mangled up when he unloaded the truck in his yard, was fixed up nicely after several failed attempts at pulling it back into its original shape with his tractor. He pulled, then hammered it down.
Brad tows it away with his tractor, with assistance from a stray cat that is probably looking for a home for her kittens soon to be born. Her favorite place turns out to be the bench seat inside the cabin. Can't blame her!
However, the cat did not help with anything but a scrutinizing look before Brad realized he used chains that were too short, and the truck did not have enough space to stop after he braked, and it stopped right in the tractor's bucket, which slightly damaged the hood that was already severely bitten by rust.
Photo: Grit & Iron Garage Power washing alone wasn’t enough to clean the light-blue truck, given the thick moss blanketing the hood and the layer of mold covering almost everything else. Brad resorted to hand-scrubbing decades of grime and organic growth embedded into the body panels. It’s dirty work, but somebody's got to do it. His son Joey jumped in to lend a hand, proving to be far more helpful than the cat.
" I t looks like pretty cool-looking patina ," he concludes. However, it's not just rust that makes the hood look scarlet, but also moss that grew over the decades in which the truck sat untouched in someone's yard. However, removing everything that grew on the paint comes off with the paint.
The first wash (several washes, actually) in decades is just the beginning. Brad plans to make it run and drive, so it probably won't take long before it hits the road again for the first time in nearly 40 years.

Once America’s most popular electric pickup, the Ford F-150 Lightning is finding a second life on the used market.
Ford F-150 Lightning finds buyers in the used market
The F-150 Lightning is hard to pass up at 50% to 60% off sticker price, even used. With new models no longer available , Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes on the used market.
After the last model rolled off the assembly line last December, CEO Jim Farley said the decision to end production came as the “very high-end EVs, the $50K, 70K, $80,000 vehicles, they just weren’t selling.”
At 50% to 60% off, it now looks like a bargain in the used market. “When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale EV dealer, recently told Bloomberg .

On the used market, however, “the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot,” he added.
Used Ford F-150 Lightnings are selling in about 20 days, less than half the 44-day average for used vehicles in the US. According to Edmunds.com , prices are now up 4% to about $50,000 since the start of the year.
2024 Ford F-150 Lightning Platinum Black (Source: Ford)
Douglass said that close to one-third of used models are sold by rival dealerships that would normally flip them back to Ford. However, many are opting to sell them directly because of demand.
Chase Norris from Colorado called the electric pickup a bargain. He purchased a used Lightning for around $40,000 and considers it a major upgrade from his previous gas F-150.
EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence, which sells pre-owned electric vehicles, said he can’t get his hands on any reasonably priced used F-150 Lightnings currently.
Ford F-150 Lightning, Mustang Mach-E at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Ford)
He said many Lightning buyers use it as a second truck to save money during their weekly commute.
It looks essentially the same as the gas-powered F-150, offers instant torque, and produces zero tailpipe emissions, but the electric pickup failed to meet Ford’s expectations because of its higher price.
The base F-150 Lightning Pro debuted in 2021 with a starting MSRP of $39,974, but that was quickly raised to around $60,000 a year or so later.
2024 Ford F-150 Lightning Flash (Source: Ford)
According to Edmunds.com , the average transaction price for the F-150 Lightning in its first year of sales was $79,000 because Ford focused on higher-priced trims. The gas version’s ATP was about $19,000 less.
Even with the higher sticker price, Ford was losing a considerable amount on each Lightning it produced. In Q1 2024, Ford lost more than $100,000 on every EV it built.
Next year, Ford will take another crack at the electric pickup market with the Fathom, the first vehicle based on its “groundbreaking” new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Ford said the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard-range version. Even with the $1,595 delivery fee included, the electric pickup will start at under $30,000.
As the first vehicle built on its UEV platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step-change from its first-generation EVs.
According to Ford, the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 and will be the first vehicle with Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.
Ford’s midsize UEV pickup spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Reddit)
We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger this summer.
Ford reportedly aims to sell around 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week that the launch remains on track for Q4 2027.
Farley called the Fathom a “breakthrough product” and said that the MSRP under $30,000 is perfect for today’s market.
At least some F-150 owners are already trading in for lower-priced options. A member of the Ford F-150 Lightning Owners Group, JF, said that although it was a great ride, “Carvana gave us just a little less than we paid new,” adding, “R2, here we come!”
When Torque News reached out, JF said he “really liked the Lightning,” but wanted something smaller. “With the current increase in resale value, the time to trade seemed right,” JF added.

Like many equipment brands, German forklift maker Jungheinrich has been struggling to crack the Asian industrial markets – but the company is set to change all that with the launch of a new line of 1.6- to 3-ton class electric forklifts designed specifically to navigate the region’s tight warehouses and factories.
Jungheinrich launched the next generation of its EFG MB and MC electric counterbalance forklifts, giving businesses more flexibility to match truck performance with the battery options, charging systems, and operator features that meet their specific needs .
“Different operations have different requirements,” said Lisa Jing Xue, Managing Director at Jungheinrich’s Qingpu Plant, China. “With the EFG M series, customers can configure the (forklift) truck around their application, workload and operators – whether they need greater maneuverability for confined warehouse spaces, or a stable, powerful truck for demanding transport and stacking work.”
Forklift buyers can choose between two performance packages, prioritizing energy efficiency for everyday material handling or more driving and lifting muscle for more demanding, high-throughput operations. The higher-performance package comes standard on models rated for 2.5-3.0 tons, with a choice of either lead-acid or lithium-ion batteries with 346 or 690 Ah of capacity available to suit different workloads and shift patterns. Both ship with regenerative braking tech that can recover up to 30% of the energy used in stopping and lowering loads , too, helping to keep these machines running longer between charging sessions.

Mission-focused forklifts
Jungheinrich EFG M launch photo.
“We carried out extensive customer research to understand what the market needs,” added Jing Xue. “Customers can invest in the performance required today and add further capabilities as their application demands.”
Optional features include fingertip controls, a larger 4″ digital display, upgraded LED lighting, and operator-assistance (ADAS) systems , while flexible seating and cabin configurations are designed to keep drivers comfortable through long shifts. A slim B-pillar and glass roof help visibility in busy warehouses , while the four-wheel EFG MC gets automatic cornering speed reduction as standard. Integrated telematics are also standard, giving fleet managers access to utilization data, maintenance planning and pre-operational checks from day one.
Jungheinrich says the order books for both the three- and four-wheel electric forklifts are open now, ready to be supported by the company’s 6,000+ person strong service network across the Asia-Pacific region.

Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries .
The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.
Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act ( DERA ) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support , customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion . Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.
As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money .
Advertisement - scroll for more content
“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”
Loads of promise
Janus electric semi in Australia; by Janus Electric.
The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment . That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.
“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

source_document.body:
AI
Workstation
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Front 4
With several partners in its DGX Station initiative, NVIDIA’s project to bring its server-grade Grace Blackwell GB300 hardware to desktop workstations has no shortage of hardware suppliers. Or system designs, for that matter. Of all of these, Supermicro is a clear frontrunner for the most interesting workstation, thanks to its unique, convertible design.
Today we are taking a look at our latest DGX Station system with Supermicro’s Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC). By squeezing in as much compute hardware as a 1.6kW power supply can sustain, NVIDIA and its partners are positioning these systems as the ultimate desk-side AI boxes for local AI work.
Supermicro Super AI Station (ARS-511GD-NB-LCC) Key Specs
CPU | NVIDIA Grace 72-Core Neoverse V2 (72C/72T)
GPU | NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra
Operating System | Ubuntu 24.04 LTS with NVIDIA AI Developer Tools
Memory | CPU: 496GB LPDDR5X (396GB/s) GPU: 252GB HBM3E (7.1TB/s)
Storage | 2x M.2 2280 (PCIe Gen6 x4) 2x M.2 2280 (PCIe Gen5 x4)
Video Card | Optional: NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell 2000/4000/6000
PSU | 1600W (80 PLUS Titanium)
Form Factor | Tower Workstation (5U) 218 x 455 x 701 mm (8.6 x 17.9 x 27.6 in)
Networking | 2x 400Gbps (QSFP112, ConnectX-8) 10Gb Ethernet (RJ45, Marvell) 1Gb Ethernet (BMC)
Ports | Front: 2x USB-A 5Gbps Rear: 4x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x USB Micro-B UART (BMC), 2x 400GbE (QSFP112), 1x 10GbE LAN (RJ45, Marvell), 1x 1GbE LAN (RJ45, BMC), 3x 3.5mm Audio, 1x Mini DisplayPort (BMC)
Meanwhile, every DGX Station vendor is putting their own spin on how a GB300 desktop should be built, and Supermicro is no different. For Supermicro, that means taking the “server at your desk” motif a little more literally than most, by developing a system that can either be set up as a full-size desktop tower or placed in a rack as a 5U system. It is, without a doubt, quintessentially Supermicro and a great example of how the company has applied its server expertise to the workstation market. It also makes a lot of sense given what we have learned with the networking on these systems.
Without further ado, let us dive right in.
Supermicro Super AI Station External Hardware Overview
The first time you see Supermicro’s Super AI Server, it is immediately obvious that it is different from the full-tower PCs other DGX Station vendors offer. For their own DGX Station system, Supermicro has done the most Supermicro thing possible by putting the system inside of a convertible chassis. This system can be set up as a desktop workstation, or it can be put on rails and rack-mounted as a 5U server.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Side 3
That kind of convertible design has a huge impact on the system design, as we will see. Both the system’s form factor and internal layout have been optimized to fulfill both roles, which at times makes this a very different system from other DGX Station systems.
One immediate impact of that design is that the Super AI Station is a bit shorter and much deeper than a typical PC tower workstation. At 455mm tall, the Super AI Station is skinny enough to fit between a pair of rack posts. The trade-off is that it is 701mm (or nearly 28 inches) long.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Front 1
With 1600 watts of hardware to cool, the Super AI Station is best described as a high-airflow system. Almost every square millimeter of space on the front of the system is dedicated to drawing in air to cool the system.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Front IO 1
The sole exception to that is a small front I/O panel, which, despite the heavy airflow emphasis, marks the first time we have seen an actual front I/O panel on a DGX Station. Supermicro’s server roots make themselves apparent here once again, as the port collection is a simple pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports. Compared with other systems, we have seen other vendors put 10Gbps USB-A and USB-C ports here, underscoring the server roots of this design once more. The ports themselves are adequately labeled, but it feels a bit more like a server in this respect.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Power Button 1
Otherwise, the front I/O panel is rounded out with the power button, a smaller reset button, and finally a drive activity LED. The system status LED is embedded in the power button and can illuminate red or blue, depending on the system status.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Front Latch 1
To the left of the front I/O panel is a locked cage, which hides the system’s service tag information. This area could also theoretically house front panel storage expansion.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Side 1
As for the sides of the Super AI Station, both sides are unremarkable. Unlike Supermicro’s fun demo unit back at Computex , the production hardware does not come with a plexiglass window. If you want to see inside, you will have to take the side panels off. Since the system is convertible, Supermicro doesn’t rely on the sides for significant ventilation, so these panels are little more than simple steel sheets.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Rear 1
Flipping over to the rear of the system, we finally get a better idea of just how different the Super AI Station is from more standard workstations: this is not a standard EEB/E-ATX chassis. The power supply is on its own side of the system, there is an obvious coolant tank, and, though not obvious in this shot, the motherboard is installed upside-down. The PCIe slot brackets are at the top of the system.
Because NVIDIA provides the motherboards for all these DGX Station systems, the port layout is standardized, so Supermicro’s matches the other vendors.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-QSFP 400Gb LAN Ports 1
Starting on the left, the system’s two QSFP112 ports are fed by the powerful NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC. Each port offers 400Gbps networking and is the primary way the system connects to high-speed storage and/or other DGX Station-based systems. We have shown that these systems can push 800Gbps through the NIC in certain circumstances. The ConnectX-8 SuperNIC driving these ports does a lot of heavy lifting beyond networking, and the capabilities and limitations of these QSFP ports are somewhat complex as a result (more on this in a bit). Meanwhile, there is a grate above the QSFP cages to allow for a bit more airflow for cooling.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Rear IO 1
For more mundane networking use cases, the system also has a pair of RJ45 Ethernet jacks. The left 1G port connects to the BMC and is for system management. OpenBMC handles management via an HTML5 iKVM. The RJ45 jack on the right side is a 10Gb Ethernet port powered by Marvell’s tried-and-true 10GbE controller. The system topology is fascinating. Marvell’s 10Gbase-T controller is attached to the NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNIC’s built-in PCIe switch, then to the CPU. It does not connect directly to the CPU.
Below are the remaining USB ports. These four ports all run at 10Gbps, making these the fastest USB ports on the system. This also means that since NVIDIA did not include USB-C ports in its motherboard design, you will not find any USB-C ports on the Super AI Station.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Audio Ports 1
To the right, we have a trio of audio jacks for two-channel audio out, plus separate mic and line-in jacks.
At the end of the rear I/O panel, two more ports connect to the BMC. On the left is a serial UART in a micro-USB form factor. To the right is a Mini DisplayPort output from the BMC for system management and configuration. DGX Station systems do not have a true integrated display GPU (Blackwell Ultra is more of a compute accelerator), so the BMC provides the only out-of-the-box graphics output. For a full-featured graphics solution, you can pair DGX Station systems with a compatible NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell video card. In this case, Supermicro has included an RTX PRO 2000 Blackwell card.
Notably, no port is labeled on the rear of the system. Supermicro has seemingly opted not to print anything on its I/O shield, at least in this example. For a server, this is par for the course, but as the Super AI Station is meant to double as a workstation, it would have been nice to see. We have an early system, so sometimes those early systems miss details like that.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Coolant Tank 1
Like all DGX Station systems, the Super AI Station is liquid-cooled. Supermicro’s design makes this obvious. The company uses an externally accessible coolant tank mounted toward the top of the system. Because the system comes completely pre-built, the Super AI Station is designed for minimal maintenance, so the externally accessible tank seems like a holdover from data center systems that can require more active maintenance. Regardless, if the system starts running low on coolant, the liquid level indicator makes it easy to see, and there are ports for filling and draining the system.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-1600W Platinum Level Power Supply 1
Elsewhere, near the bottom of the system, we have the Super AI Station’s 1600 Watt power supply. While the wattage is standardized across DGX Station systems, the actual power supply model is not. This benefits Supermicro, as theirs is the first DGX Station system to cross our labs with an 80 Plus Titanium-rated power supply, one step higher than the Platinum units we have seen in other systems.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Top 1
Because Supermicro put all of their front I/O and buttons on the front of the system, there is no need for the top of the system to be anything special. Coupled with the fact that it has no ventilation here, since that would not work in a rackmount scenario, Supermicro is keeping things simple on top. This top can be popped off to expose mounting points for rackmount rails.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Bottom 1
The bottom, for that matter. Here it is much more obvious, even in a workstation configuration, that this chassis can be rack-mounted, as you can easily see where the rails would go.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Feet 1
This also means that for workstation mode, the chassis needs a pair of feet attached to properly support the system and its copious 88lb weight.
Supermicro ARS-511GD-NB-LCC Super AI Station-Feet 2
That wraps things up for our outside look at the Super AI Station. For the rest of the story, let us dive into the system’s chassis, where this gets very different.
